topic: Outdated Course Content & Lack of Real-World Relevance
sub_point_text: As a 4th-year student from the old curriculum, I find that courses like CSC325, CSC340, and CSC319 are outdated and do not meet real-world work needs. The content, which currently focuses on GUI development and restructuring, is quite old. To make Java more practically useful, these courses should involve building a full Desktop Application or doing a Big Data project instead.
original_full_text:
As a 4th-year student from the old curriculum, in my perspective I’m judging based on (quality / attending one class session) and only on the knowledge gained in class, not outside the classroom. My opinions are as follows:

1. Some courses do not meet the needs of real-world work because they are outdated, such as CSC325, CSC340, and CSC319. In my view, these courses should teach more than just GUI development and restructuring. I think the content is quite old. To make Java more practically useful, it should involve building a full Desktop Application or doing a Big Data project instead.

2. Courses that should be hands-on ended up being mostly theoretical. For example, CSC220 was very disappointing for me in terms of learning networking. I believe this subject has huge potential for further development, but it felt like there was a lot of talk and not much substance. We pay almost 50,000 baht to sit in an old CB building without doing any concrete lab work, unlike other faculties that pay less but have proper networking workshops. Meanwhile, we just sit there, looking at each other, after paying tens of thousands more but receiving lower quality than other departments.

CSC325 was also disappointing. I believe this course still has potential and could offer much more. There was no project at all. Most of the time was spent grinding through SeedLab, documenting it, and then taking the final exam. In the end, there was no real continuation or application. I see this course as almost useful — it was just missing a focus on quality, as it emphasized quantity of work instead.

3. There was a gap in coding practice. During Years 1–2, it was the most stressful period, but also the most beneficial for me. However, in Years 3–4, I felt like coding almost completely disappeared. It became very theory-heavy, with not much hands-on practice. I understand that this might be due to the reasons mentioned in points 1 and 2. I also feel that this may have already been improved in the new curriculum. Overall, though, I found the learning experience enjoyable during my time here.

Not only it’s not useful it’s also waste of my time and energy to attend all those courses In Jarah course, I don’t understand why LINE is consistently used as the main communication channel for assignments, class materials, and important course details. LINE has limited message history accessibility and is not a professional or reliable platform for managing academic information.
Using LINE for quick reminders or minor announcements is acceptable. But relying on it for all course-related communication is excessive and problematic. The faculty already provides proper platforms such as Microsoft Teams and CSCMS, which are designed for structured communication, assignment posting, and long-term record keeping.

Assignments communicated verbally in class, through chat messages, or by asking students to take notes are subjective and lack clarity. As a result, many students are uncertain about task requirements, deadlines, and expectations.
Assignments and course materials should be consistently posted on Microsoft Teams or CSCMS in a clear, concrete, and centralized manner. This would significantly reduce misunderstandings and help students manage their work more effectively.

topic: Information Dissemination Challenges for International Students
sub_point_text: Important academic and opportunity-related information, such as details about the Taiwan internship or related programs, does not always reach Burmese students and other international students in a timely or clear manner. This information gap creates inequality in access to opportunities and leaves students unsure about whom to contact for guidance or clarification, especially when students from other international majors have already been preparing for similar opportunities since the previous semester.
original_full_text:
Important academic and opportunity-related information does not always reach Burmese students (or other international students) in a timely or clear manner. For example, information about the Taiwan internship or related programs was not well communicated, while students from other international majors had already been preparing since the previous semester. This information gap creates inequality in access to opportunities and leaves students unsure about whom to contact for guidance or clarification.
I hope the SIT International Relations office can be more proactive in sharing information about exchange programs and overseas internships. The Faculty of Engineering and Science has its own International Affairs office, which is very active in regularly posting and announcing overseas opportunities. In comparison, SIT IR has been relatively quiet, and some students are not even aware that the office exists.
If workload or capacity is an issue, perhaps the university could consider hiring additional staff or involving student assistants to help with outreach and communication.
